Next month, the 26th will mark the one-year anniversary of the Tai Po Wang Fuk Court fire. The independent committee investigating the fire is expected to submit its report to the Chief Executive before the end of October. Recent reports indicated that the government has activated the Head of Department Accountability System to investigate administrative responsibility for the fire, with policy officials redeployed to assist. Chief Executive John Lee today (the 6th) did not confirm whether the mechanism has been activated, stating that the government has made a series of arrangements and will implement reforms and pursue accountability as soon as possible after the report is submitted. The luxury residence One Stanley in Stanley was revealed to have reinforcing steel that did not match the plans. Lee stated that the Buildings Department is investigating the case and he has requested the Development Bureau to oversee the investigation. With multiple projects being exposed for problems one after another, he emphasised that the construction quality of Hong Kong's building works is of great importance, relating to the professionalism, quality and safety of Hong Kong's construction industry, and the government will strictly enforce the law.

It is nearly a year since the Wang Fuk Court fire, and the independent committee is expected to submit its report before the end of October. (File photo)

Earlier media reports indicated that two policy officials—former Deputy Secretary for Security Mok Kwan-yu and Commissioner for Sports Choi Kin-bun—would provide support at the investigation group under the Public Service Commission, specifically responsible for preliminary work on administrative accountability.

Chief Executive John Lee attended a press meeting before the Executive Council meeting today, and was asked whether the reports were true. He was also asked whether activating the Head of Department Accountability System to investigate responsibility means that even if there is a report, any accountability involving officials would not have immediate results, and how long the public would have to wait.

Lee stated that he had made it clear from the start that after the independent committee submits its report, he would actively study and follow up on its recommendations, carry out reforms and announce details. He did not directly respond to whether policy officials had been redeployed to prepare preliminary investigation work, only saying that "the government has made a series of arrangements during this period," emphasising that after the report is submitted, based on its content, "comprehensive reforms will be implemented and accountability pursued as soon as possible in the short term," with a detailed announcement to follow.

Lee stated that after the independent committee submits its report, reforms will be implemented and accountability pursued as soon as possible based on the report's content. (File photo)

Lee also reiterated that improvement measures are urgent, and therefore when delivering the Policy Address in September, he had announced seven priority improvement measures, including: prohibiting smoking at construction sites, strengthening regulation of fire service installations, enhancing disciplinary action and punishment for professionals and contractors, improving compliance in owners' corporations, studying the criminalisation of bid-rigging, providing tendering and tender evaluation services for the first time, establishing prequalification lists for consultants and contractors, and researching measures to better assist members of the public on the professional aspects of building works.

According to records, the Public Service Commission is an independent statutory advisory body that advises the Chief Executive on civil service appointment, promotion and discipline matters. The Head of Department Accountability System was introduced by Chief Executive Lee in last year's Policy Address, establishing a two-tier investigation mechanism based on the severity of departmental issues. If the issue is less serious in nature or involves an isolated incident, the head of department will conduct a first-tier investigation. If a department has serious problems, or involves extensive, recurring systemic issues, or may involve the role of the head of department, an investigation group led by the Public Service Commission will conduct a second-tier investigation.

The luxury residence One Stanley was revealed to have units with reinforcing steel that did not match the plans. Lee stated that he would not comment on the case while it is still under investigation, and he has asked the Development Bureau to oversee the Buildings Department's investigation.

One Stanley reinforcing steel issue – Development Bureau asked to oversee investigation

Recently, building works have been exposed for problems one after another, including lift shaft tilting at the new block of Queen Mary Hospital, concrete samples at a Tung Chung public housing estate not meeting strength standards, and floor slab reinforcing steel at the Stanley luxury residence One Stanley not matching the plans. When asked whether there were problems with construction or even project supervision, Lee responded:

In response to the One Stanley project issue, he stated that the Buildings Department is seriously investigating the case, "examining whether construction quality and supervision have been adequate, and will handle it strictly in accordance with the law." As the investigation is still ongoing, he would not comment on the case, and has asked the Development Bureau to oversee the investigation. However, he emphasised that he attaches great importance to the construction quality of Hong Kong's building works, "paying attention to whether professionals related to the projects have diligently supervised, and whether contractors have violated regulations during construction." He also noted that this concerns the professionalism, quality and safety of Hong Kong's construction industry, and the government will definitely enforce the law strictly.

He has also asked the Development Bureau to enhance regulatory requirements and penalties under the law for building works in general, ensuring that the legislation has sufficient deterrent effect, severely punishing those responsible for violations, and safeguarding the professionalism, quality and safety of Hong Kong's building works. The Development Bureau will submit proposed amendments to the Buildings Ordinance this year, strengthening regulation and enhancing the disciplinary system and penalties, and the authorities will press ahead with the work at full speed.

The difficulty faced by nursing graduates in finding jobs has recently attracted attention. Lee stated that the demand for nurses has always existed long-term, and noted that the Hospital Authority currently has over 3,000 nursing vacancies that graduates can apply for. (File photo)

Executive Councillor Cheung Yueman criticises "unions impersonating people" – Lee says demand has long existed

Discussions about nurses' difficulty in finding employment have heated up recently. The trigger was a phone-in programme on a radio station after the Policy Address, in which a Mr Kwok, who claimed to be a psychiatric nurse in a disciplinary force, said his application for deferred retirement was not approved, and that his nursing graduate daughter was unemployed upon graduation. He questioned the Hospital Authority's recruitment of Mainland medical staff. Executive Councillor Cheung Yueman subsequently questioned whether the union was "possibly having people impersonate members to make calls," and expressed his full support for importing talent from outside.

When asked by reporters how to address the difficulty faced by nursing graduates in finding jobs, and how to resolve the concentration of vacancies among senior nurses, and how to respond to remarks by the Executive Councillor that were said to have intensified social divisions, Lee said that in every industry, there are situations where graduates do not seek employment immediately after graduation due to individual reasons, or where hiring organisations select those best suited to their needs, "and individual cases of people not being hired will arise." He emphasised that the community's demand for nurses has always existed, particularly given Hong Kong's continuously developing medical services and an ageing population, "so the recruitment numbers will ultimately necessarily reflect these existing demands." Without naming anyone, he also noted that "there are different discussions in society on this aspect, which can help everyone clarify the issues."

Lee also stated that according to 2025/26 figures, there are approximately 4,000 potential nursing graduates, with about 2,500 actually applying to the Hospital Authority—meaning 1,500 applied for positions outside the Hospital Authority—while the Hospital Authority currently still has over 3,000 nursing vacancies, "nursing graduates can apply, and there is a chance of being hired."

Secretary for Health Professor Lo Chung-mau earlier accepted interviews with multiple media outlets to clarify that the government's recruitment policy definitely prioritises local talent. Lee also reiterated that based on the Hospital Authority's existing nursing workforce, "99.8% are locally trained nurses in Hong Kong," clearly implementing the local-talent-first recruitment policy. He also noted that currently 40% of nurses work in the public healthcare system, with the remaining 60% in other healthcare positions, such as community nursing, elderly care, rehabilitation services, and private medical institutions. He emphasised that the community's long-term demand for nurses exists, and the government will, according to medical service needs, exchange views with the industry and academia, and make good plans for healthcare training and workforce development.
